```{r global-options, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(patchwork)
library(kableExtra)

tidymodels_prefer()

set.seed(567)
num_pts <- 20
x1 <- runif(num_pts, 0, 10)
x2 <- runif(num_pts, 0, 10) 
y1 <- 4*x1 - 1 + rnorm(num_pts, 0, 8)
y2 <- 4*x1 - 1 + rnorm(num_pts, 0, 30)

num_new <- 10
x1_new <- runif(num_new, 0, 10)
x2_new <- runif(num_new, 0, 10)
y1_new <- 4*x1_new - 1 + rnorm(num_new, 0, 8)

data <- tibble(
  x1 = x1,
  x2 = x2,
  y = y1
)

lr_plot_spec <- linear_reg() 
lr_plot_rec <- recipe(y ~ x1, data = data)
lr_plot_wf <- workflow() %>%
  add_model(lr_plot_spec) %>%
  add_recipe(lr_plot_rec)
lr_plot_fit <- lr_plot_wf %>%
  fit(data)
```

## The Highlights

+ Are our models useful?

  + Global tests for model utility
  + Tests on individual model terms
  + Confidence intervals for coefficients

+ Intervals for Model Predictions

  + Confidence intervals for a *mean* response
  + Prediction intervals for an *individual* response
  
:::{.fragment}

**Note:** While statistical inference techniques will be more present in our ***statistical learning*** settings, we'll still need some of them in the ***machine learning*** setting. 

:::

:::{.fragment}

In particular, we should have no expectation that our models make perfectly accurate predictions. We'll need to report intervals within which we expect a future observation to fall, and then perhaps make further use of those intervals if we wish to report a singular value.

:::

## Statistical Learning Reminders

<div style="font-size:17pt">

:::{.fragment}

In the statistical learning context, we come with a hypothesized model form:

:::

:::{.fragment}

$$y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \cdots + \beta_k x_k + \varepsilon$$

<center> or, equivalently...</center>


$$\mathbb{E}\left[y\right] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \cdots + \beta_k x_k$$

:::

:::{.fragment}

Proposing such a model comes with several questions -- one global (about the model as a whole), and potentially many local (about individual model terms).

:::

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}

:::{.fragment}

<center> **Global Test for Model Utility** </center>

:::

:::{.fragment}

**Intuitive Version:** Does my model have any explanatory value at all?

:::

:::{.fragment}

**Formal Hypotheses:** $\begin{array}{lcl} H_{0} & : & \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \cdots = \beta_k = 0\\ H_{a} & : & \text{At least one explanatory variable has a}\\ & & \text{non-zero coefficient}\end{array}$

:::

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}

:::{.fragment}

<center> **Local, Term-Based Tests** </center>

:::

:::{.fragment}

**Intuitive Version:** Does this particular model term provide explanatory value, given all of the other model terms?

:::

:::{.fragment}

**Formal Hypotheses:** <br/>$\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 & : & \beta_{~i} = 0\\ H_a & : & \beta_{~i} \neq 0\end{array}$

:::

:::

::::

</div>

## For You to Try

<div style="font-size:17pt">

:::{.fragment}

Before moving on, in your Quarto Document, assume we're in a statistical learning context and we have reason to believe $y$ is linearly associated with `x1`, `x2`, `x3`, and `x4`. Try the following:

:::

1. Write out the proposed model form.
2. Write out the hypotheses for the *Global Test of Model Utility*.
3. How many individual term-based tests are there? Write the hypotheses for all of them.
4. Use the `{tidymodels}` framework to construct the linear regression model.

</div>

<div style="font-size:15pt">

:::{.fragment}

*Solution.*

:::

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}

:::{.fragment}

**Model Form:**

$$\mathbb{E}\left[y\right] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 x_3 + \beta_4 x_4$$

:::

:::{.fragment}

**Global Test for Model Utility:**

$$\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 & : & \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \beta_3 = \beta_4 = 0\\ H_a & : & \text{At least one of the coefficient } \beta \text{s is non-zero}\end{array}$$

:::

:::{.fragment}

**Term-Based Tests:**

$$\begin{array}{l} H_0 : \beta_1 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_1 \neq 0\end{array}~~~\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 : \beta_2 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_2 \neq 0\end{array}~~~\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 : \beta_3 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_3 \neq 0\end{array}~~~\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 : \beta_4 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_4 \neq 0\end{array}$$

:::

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}

:::{.fragment}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

lr_spec <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm")

lr_rec <- recipe(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4, 
                 data = toy_data)

lr_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_model(lr_spec) |>
  add_recipe(lr_rec)

lr_fit <- lr_wf |>
  fit(toy_data)
```

:::

:::

::::

</div>

## Carrying Out the Tests

<div style="font-size:14pt">

:::{.fragment}

**Global Test for Model Utility:** This is an ANOVA test, which we can run by piping our fitted model object (`lr_fit`) into `glance()`.

:::

:::{.fragment}

**Individual Term-Based Tests:** These individual tests are $t$-tests and can be run by piping our fitted model object (`lr_fit`) into `tidy()`.

:::

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}

:::{.fragment}

**Model Form:**

$$\mathbb{E}\left[y\right] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 x_3 + \beta_4 x_4$$

**Global Test for Model Utility:**

$$\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 & : & \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \beta_3 = \beta_4 = 0\\ H_a & : & \text{At least one of the coefficient } \beta \text{s is non-zero}\end{array}$$

**Term-Based Tests:**

$$\begin{array}{l} H_0 : \beta_1 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_1 \neq 0\end{array}~~~\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 : \beta_2 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_2 \neq 0\end{array}~~~\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 : \beta_3 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_3 \neq 0\end{array}~~~\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 : \beta_4 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_4 \neq 0\end{array}$$
:::

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}

:::{.fragment}

**Let's try it!** Run the tests in your Quarto document.

:::

:::{.fragment}

<center>**Global Test for Model Utility**</center>

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

lr_fit |>
  glance()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

lr_fit |>
  glance() |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 16)
```

:::

:::{.fragment}

<center> **Term-Based Tests**</center>

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

lr_fit |>
  tidy()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

lr_fit |>
  tidy() |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 16)
```

:::

:::

::::

</div>

## Consequences of the Tests

<div style="font-size:14pt">

:::{.fragment fragment-index=1}

As long as the assumptions underlying the model construction are approximately satisfied, then the ***Global Test for Model Utility*** will tell us whether the data provides evidence to suggest that at least one of the model terms has explanatory value, and the ***Term-Based Tests*** will tell us which terms those are, controlling for the other model terms.

:::

:::{.fragment fragment-index=2}

We'll look at the modeling assumptions at our next class meeting but, for now, we'll focus on interpreting the output.

:::

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}

:::{.fragment fragment-index=3}

**Model Form:**

$$\mathbb{E}\left[y\right] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 x_3 + \beta_4 x_4$$

**Global Test for Model Utility:**

$$\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 & : & \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \beta_3 = \beta_4 = 0\\ H_a & : & \text{At least one of the coefficient } \beta \text{s is non-zero}\end{array}$$

**Term-Based Tests:**

$$\begin{array}{l} H_0 : \beta_1 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_1 \neq 0\end{array}~~~\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 : \beta_2 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_2 \neq 0\end{array}~~~\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 : \beta_3 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_3 \neq 0\end{array}~~~\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 : \beta_4 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_4 \neq 0\end{array}$$
:::

:::{.fragment fragment-index=4}

**Global Test for Model Utility:** The p-value is approximately $5.12\times 10^{-5}$, which is below $0.05$. The data suggests our model has some utility.

:::

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}

:::{.fragment fragment-index=3}

<center>**Global Test for Model Utility**</center>

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

lr_fit |>
  glance()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

lr_fit |>
  glance() |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 16)
```

<center> **Term-Based Tests**</center>

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

lr_fit |>
  tidy()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

lr_fit |>
  tidy() |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 16)
```

:::

:::

::::

:::{.fragment}

**Term-Based Tests:** The data provide evidence suggesting that `x1` and `x2` have explanatory value, but that `x3` and `x4` may not, due to their high p-values.

:::

</div>

## Consequences of the Tests (Cont'd.)

<div style="font-size:14pt">

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}

**Model Form:**

$$\mathbb{E}\left[y\right] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 x_3 + \beta_4 x_4$$

**Global Test for Model Utility:**

$$\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 & : & \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \beta_3 = \beta_4 = 0\\ H_a & : & \text{At least one of the coefficient } \beta \text{s is non-zero}\end{array}$$

**Term-Based Tests:**

$$\begin{array}{l} H_0 : \beta_1 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_1 \neq 0\end{array}~~~\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 : \beta_2 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_2 \neq 0\end{array}~~~\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 : \beta_3 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_3 \neq 0\end{array}~~~\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 : \beta_4 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_4 \neq 0\end{array}$$
**Global Test for Model Utility:** The p-value is approximately $5.12\times 10^{-5}$, which is below $0.05$. The data suggests our model has some utility.

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}

<center>**Global Test for Model Utility**</center>

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

lr_fit |>
  glance()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

lr_fit |>
  glance() |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 16)
```

<center> **Term-Based Tests**</center>

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

lr_fit |>
  tidy()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

lr_fit |>
  tidy() |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 16)
```

:::

::::

**Term-Based Tests:** The data provide evidence suggesting that `x1` and `x2` have explanatory value, but that `x3` and `x4` may not, due to their high p-values.

:::{.fragment}

**Next Action:** Since the ***Global Test for Model Utility*** indicated that our model has explanatory value but some of our explanatory variables are not statistically significant, we'll need to reduce the model.

:::

:::{.fragment}

We'll do this by removing the explanatory variable with the *least* evidence for inclusion (that's the one with the highest p-value).

:::

</div>

## Consequences of the Tests (Cont'd.)

<div style="font-size:14pt">

**Next Action:** Since the ***Global Test for Model Utility*** indicated that our model has explanatory value but some of our explanatory variables are not statistically significant, we'll need to reduce the model.

We'll do this by removing the explanatory variable with the *least* evidence for inclusion (that's the one with the highest p-value).

:::{.fragment fragment-index=1}

We'll drop `x4` from the model and re-fit it. Note that dropping one variable from the model will change all fitted coefficients, standard errors, tests statistics, p-values, and other performance metrics so ***we should only ever drop one explanatory variable at a time***.

:::

</div>

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}

<div style="font-size:12pt">

:::{.fragment fragment-index=2}

**Model Form:**

$$\mathbb{E}\left[y\right] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 x_3 \cancel{+ \beta_4 x_4}$$

**Global Test for Model Utility:**

$$\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 & : & \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \beta_3 \cancel{= \beta_4} = 0\\ H_a & : & \text{At least one of the coefficient } \beta \text{s is non-zero}\end{array}$$

**Term-Based Tests:**

$$\begin{array}{l} H_0 : \beta_1 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_1 \neq 0\end{array}~~~\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 : \beta_2 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_2 \neq 0\end{array}~~~\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 : \beta_3 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_3 \neq 0\end{array}~~~\cancel{\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 : \beta_4 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_4 \neq 0\end{array}}$$

:::

</div>

<div style="font-size:14pt">

:::{.fragment fragment-index=4}

Now we'll re-run the tests on the newly fitted model.

:::

</div>

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}

<div style="font-size:14pt">

:::{.fragment fragment-index=3}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

lr_spec <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm")

lr_rec <- recipe(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, 
                 data = toy_data)

lr_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_model(lr_spec) |>
  add_recipe(lr_rec)

lr_fit <- lr_wf |>
  fit(toy_data)
```

:::

</div>

:::

::::

## Consequences of the Tests (Cont'd.)

<div style="font-size:14pt">

**Next Action:** Since the ***Global Test for Model Utility*** indicated that our model has explanatory value but some of our explanatory variables are not statistically significant, we'll need to reduce the model.

We'll do this by removing the explanatory variable with the *least* evidence for inclusion (that's the one with the highest p-value).

We'll drop `x4` from the model and re-fit it. Note that dropping one variable from the model will change all fitted coefficients, standard errors, tests statistics, p-values, and other performance metrics so ***we should only ever drop one explanatory variable at a time***.

</div>

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}

<div style="font-size:12pt">

**Model Form:**

$$\mathbb{E}\left[y\right] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 x_3 \cancel{+ \beta_4 x_4}$$

**Global Test for Model Utility:**

$$\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 & : & \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \beta_3 \cancel{= \beta_4} = 0\\ H_a & : & \text{At least one of the coefficient } \beta \text{s is non-zero}\end{array}$$

**Term-Based Tests:**

$$\begin{array}{l} H_0 : \beta_1 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_1 \neq 0\end{array}~~~\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 : \beta_2 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_2 \neq 0\end{array}~~~\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 : \beta_3 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_3 \neq 0\end{array}~~~\cancel{\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 : \beta_4 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_4 \neq 0\end{array}}$$

</div>

<div style="font-size:14pt">

Now we'll re-run the tests on the newly fitted model.

:::{.fragment fragment-index=3}

**Results:** Notice that the p-value corresponding to `x3` still fails to indicate statistical significance. We'll remove it and refit the model.

:::

</div>

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}

<div style="font-size:14pt">

:::{.fragment fragment-index=1}

<center> **Global Test for Model Utility**</center>

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

lr_fit |>
  glance()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

lr_fit |>
  glance() |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 14)
```

:::

:::{.fragment fragment-index=2}

<center> **Term-Based Tests**</center>

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

lr_fit |>
  tidy()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

lr_fit |>
  tidy() |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 14)
```

:::

</div>

:::

::::

## Consequences of the Tests (Cont'd.)

<div style="font-size:14pt">

**Next Action:** Since the ***Global Test for Model Utility*** indicated that our model has explanatory value but some of our explanatory variables are not statistically significant, we'll need to reduce the model.

The p-value corresponding to `x3` still fails to indicate statistical significance. We'll remove it, refit, and reassess the model.

</div>

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}

<div style="font-size:12pt">

**Model Form:**

$$\mathbb{E}\left[y\right] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 \cancel{+ \beta_3 x_3} \cancel{+ \beta_4 x_4}$$

**Global Test for Model Utility:**

$$\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 & : & \beta_1 = \beta_2 \cancel{= \beta_3} \cancel{= \beta_4} = 0\\ H_a & : & \text{At least one of the coefficient } \beta \text{s is non-zero}\end{array}$$

**Term-Based Tests:**

$$\begin{array}{l} H_0 : \beta_1 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_1 \neq 0\end{array}~~~\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 : \beta_2 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_2 \neq 0\end{array}~~~\cancel{\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 : \beta_3 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_3 \neq 0\end{array}}~~~\cancel{\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 : \beta_4 = 0\\ H_a : \beta_4 \neq 0\end{array}}$$

</div>

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}

<div style="font-size:14pt">

:::{.fragment fragment-index=1}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

lr_spec <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm")

lr_rec <- recipe(y ~ x1 + x2, data = toy_data)

lr_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_model(lr_spec) |>
  add_recipe(lr_rec)

lr_fit <- lr_wf |>
  fit(toy_data)
```

:::

:::{.fragment fragment-index=4}

**Conclusion:** The explanatory variables `x3` and `x4` failed to be statistically significant. The estimated model is:

$$\mathbb{E}\left[y\right] \approx -708.23 + 4.06x_1 + 5.85x_2$$

:::

</div>

:::

::::

<div style="font-size:14pt">

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}

:::{.fragment fragment-index=2}

<center> **Global Test for Model Utility**</center>

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

lr_fit |>
  glance()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

lr_fit |>
  glance() |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 14)
```

:::

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}

:::{.fragment fragment-index=3}

<center> **Term-Based Tests**</center>

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

lr_fit |>
  tidy()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

lr_fit |>
  tidy() |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 14)
```

:::

:::

::::

</div>

## Global Test for Model Utility in Pictures

<div style="font-size:16pt">

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}

:::{.fragment fragment-index=3}

**Note:** The plots below are simplified versions for viewing -- in general, our [multiple] linear regression models will create a surface rather than a line.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-align: center
#| fig.height: 9

p1 <- toy_data |>
  ggplot() + 
  geom_point(aes(x = x1, y = y),
             size = 3) + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(toy_data$y), 
             color = "red", 
             linetype = "dashed", 
             lwd = 2) +
  geom_smooth(aes(x = x1, y = y),
              method = "lm",
              color = "blue",
              se = FALSE) + 
  labs(title = "Scenario A",
       x = "x1",
       y = "y")

p2 <- toy_data |>
  ggplot() + 
  geom_point(aes(x = x3, y = y),
             size = 3) + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(toy_data$y), 
             color = "red", 
             linetype = "dashed", 
             lwd = 2) +
  geom_smooth(aes(x = x3, y = y),
              method = "lm",
              color = "blue",
              se = FALSE) + 
  labs(title = "Scenario B",
       x = "x3",
       y = "y")

p1 / p2
```

:::

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}

:::{.fragment fragment-index=1}

$$\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 & : & \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \cdots = \beta_k = 0\\
H_a & : & \text{At least one } \beta_i \text{ is non-zero}\end{array}$$

:::

:::{.fragment fragment-index=2}

Are our *sloped* models better (more justifiable) models than the horizontal line?

:::

+ *Sloped* models use predictor information
+ Horizontal models just predict average response, ignoring all observation-specific features

  + They assume that having information about features of an observation gives no advantage in predicting/explaining its response

::: 

::::

</div>

## Additional Global Metrics from `glance()`

:::{.fragment}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

lr_fit |>
  glance()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

lr_fit |>
  glance() |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 16)
```

:::

<div style="font-size:15pt">

:::{.fragment}

The output from `glance()`ing at our fitted model object gives lots of additional information about overall model fit and quality.

:::

+ The R-squared value (`r.squared`) measures *the proportion of variation in the response variable which is explained by the terms in our fitted model*.

  + "About 60.45% of the variation in `y` is explained by linear relationships with `x1` and `x2` (our model)."
+ The *adjusted* R-squared value (`adj.r.squared`) is a better measure for comparing models than R-squared because *adjusted* R-squared penalizes the inclusion of additional model terms, while R-squared never decreases with additional terms.
+ The `sigma` value is our *residual standard error*, which is roughly the typical size of a residual (prediction error). It is often referred to as a biased measure because it is too optimistic (estimated from the data the model was trained on).

  + Considering the data our model was trained on, we expect a typical prediction error to be about 188.6, but on new or previously unseen observations we should expect that error to be higher.
+ We won't generally consider the additional items in our course.

</div>

## Confidence Intervals (Model Coefficients)

<div style="font-size:16pt">

:::{.fragment}

Whenever we estimate a parameter using data, there is uncertainty associated with that estimate.

:::

:::{.fragment}

The $\beta$-coefficients we estimate during model fitting are parameters, and there is uncertainty associated with their values.

:::

:::{.fragment}

Each fitted coefficient is accompanied by a standard error estimate (`std.error`), which can be used to construct a confidence interval.

:::

:::{.fragment}

As a reminder, an approximate 95% confidence interval can be constructed using:

$$\left(\substack{\text{Point}\\\text{Estimate}}\right) \pm 2\cdot \left(\substack{\text{Standard}\\\text{Error}}\right)$$

:::

:::{.fragment}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

lr_fit |>
  tidy()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

lr_fit |>
  tidy() |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 16)
```

:::

:::{.fragment}

We can have R build confidence intervals for us though!

:::

</div>

## Confidence Intervals (Model Coefficients)

<div style="font-size:16pt">

Whenever we estimate a parameter using data, there is uncertainty associated with that estimate.

The $\beta$-coefficients we estimate during model fitting are parameters, and there is uncertainty associated with their values.

Each fitted coefficient is accompanied by a standard error estimate (`std.error`), which can be used to construct a confidence interval.

As a reminder, an approximate 95% confidence interval can be constructed using:

$$\left(\substack{\text{Point}\\\text{Estimate}}\right) \pm 2\cdot \left(\substack{\text{Standard}\\\text{Error}}\right)$$

We can have R build confidence intervals for us though!

:::{.fragment}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

lr_fit |>
  tidy(conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.95)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

lr_fit |>
  tidy(conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.95) |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 16)
```

:::

:::{.fragment}

**Sample Interpretation:** We are 95% confident that, holding `x2` fixed, each one-unit increase in `x1` is associated with an average increase of between about 1.66 and 6.46 units in `y`.

:::

</div>

## Model Predictions

<div style="font-size:17pt">

:::{.fragment}

When we build a model, we often want to use it to make predictions on new sets of observations (counterfactuals/hypotheticals or future occurrences).

:::

:::{.fragment}

```{r}
#| fig.height: 4

x_plot <- tibble(
  x1 = seq(0, 10, length.out = 250)
)

x_plot <- x_plot %>%
  bind_cols(
  lr_plot_fit %>%
    predict(x_plot)
  ) %>%
  bind_cols(
  lr_plot_fit %>%
    predict(x_plot,
            type = "conf_int",
            level = 0.95) %>%
    rename(.conf_lower = .pred_lower,
           .conf_upper = .pred_upper)) %>%
  bind_cols(
  lr_plot_fit %>%
    predict(x_plot,
            type = "pred_int",
            level = 0.95)
  )
  
ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = x1_new, y = y1_new)) +
  geom_line(data = x_plot,
            aes(x = x1,
                y = .pred),
            color = "blue",
            lwd = 1.25) + 
  labs(
    title = "Model Predictions",
    subtitle = "(from a different scenario, for ease of visualization)",
    x = "x",
    y = "y"
  )
```

:::

:::{.fragment}

They're all wrong!

:::

:::{.fragment}

**Solution:** We'll have two types of intervals associated with model predictions, depending on our goals. We can construct ***confidence intervals*** to capture an *average* response, or ***prediction intervals*** to capture an *individual* response (each with some degree of confidence).

:::

</div>

## Confidence Intervals (Predictions)

<div style="font-size:16pt">

:::{.fragment}

The formula for confidence intervals on predictions is complex! 

:::

:::{.fragment}

$$\displaystyle{\left(\tt{point~estimate}\right)\pm t^*_{\text{df}}\cdot \left(\substack{\text{Residual}\\ \text{Standard}\\ \text{Error}}\right)\left(\sqrt{\frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x_{new} - \bar{x})^2}{\sum{\left(x - \bar{x}\right)^2}}}\right)}$$

:::

:::{.fragment}

We'll use R to construct these intervals for us.

:::

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="45%"}

:::{.fragment}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

new_data <- tibble(
  x1 = seq(0, 10, length.out = 100)
)

new_data |>
  bind_cols(
    lr_plot_fit |> predict(new_data),
    lr_plot_fit |> predict(new_data, 
                           type = "conf_int")
  ) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = x1, ymin = .pred_lower, 
                  ymax = .pred_upper), 
              fill = "grey") +
  geom_line(aes(x = x1, y = .pred), 
            color = "blue") + 
  labs(
    title = "Model with Confidence Intervals",
    subtitle = "(for average response)",
    x = "x1",
    y = "y"
  )
  
```

:::

:::

:::{.column width="55%"}

:::{.fragment}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

new_data <- tibble(
  x1 = seq(0, 10, length.out = 100)
)

new_data |>
  bind_cols(
    lr_plot_fit |> predict(new_data),
    lr_plot_fit |> predict(new_data, type = "conf_int")
  ) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = x1, ymin = .pred_lower, ymax = .pred_upper), fill = "grey") +
  geom_line(aes(x = x1, y = .pred), color = "blue") + 
  labs(
    title = "Model with Confidence Intervals",
    subtitle = "(for average response)",
    x = "x1",
    y = "y"
  )
  
```

:::

:::{.fragment}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

new_data |>
  bind_cols(
    lr_plot_fit |> predict(new_data),
    lr_plot_fit |> predict(new_data, type = "conf_int")
  ) |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 16) |>
  scroll_box(height = "150px")
  
```

:::

:::

::::



</div>

## Prediction Intervals

<div style="font-size:15pt">

:::{.fragment}

***Confidence intervals*** are useful for capturing the *average* response given values of the explanatory/predictor variables.

:::

:::{.fragment}

Often though, we are more interested in predicting an *individual* response -- ***prediction intervals*** will do that.

:::

:::{.fragment}

There's more uncertainty associated with predicting an *individual* response than an *average* response though, so these prediction intervals will be wider than the corresponding confidence intervals.

:::

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="45%"}

:::{.fragment}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

new_data <- tibble(
  x1 = seq(0, 10, length.out = 100)
)

new_data |>
  bind_cols(
    lr_plot_fit |> predict(new_data),
    lr_plot_fit |> predict(new_data, 
                           type = "pred_int")
  ) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = x1, ymin = .pred_lower, 
                  ymax = .pred_upper), 
              fill = "grey") +
  geom_line(aes(x = x1, y = .pred), 
            color = "blue") + 
  labs(
    title = "Model with Prediction Intervals",
    subtitle = "(for individual responses)",
    x = "x1",
    y = "y"
  )
  
```

:::

:::

:::{.column width="55%"}

:::{.fragment}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

new_data <- tibble(
  x1 = seq(0, 10, length.out = 100)
)

new_data |>
  bind_cols(
    lr_plot_fit |> predict(new_data),
    lr_plot_fit |> predict(new_data, type = "pred_int")
  ) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = x1, ymin = .pred_lower, ymax = .pred_upper), fill = "grey") +
  geom_line(aes(x = x1, y = .pred), color = "blue") + 
  labs(
    title = "Model with Prediction Intervals",
    subtitle = "(for individual responses)",
    x = "x1",
    y = "y"
  )
  
```

:::

:::{.fragment}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

new_data |>
  bind_cols(
    lr_plot_fit |> predict(new_data),
    lr_plot_fit |> predict(new_data, type = "pred_int")
  ) |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 16) |>
  scroll_box(height = "150px")
  
```

:::

:::

::::

</div>

## Both Intervals Together

<div style="font-size:15pt">

***Confidence intervals*** are useful for capturing the *average* response given values of the explanatory/predictor variables.

Often though, we are more interested in predicting an *individual* response -- ***prediction intervals*** will do that.

There's more uncertainty associated with predicting an *individual* response than an *average* response though, so these prediction intervals will be wider than the corresponding confidence intervals.

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="45%"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

new_data <- tibble(
  x1 = seq(0, 10, length.out = 100)
)

new_data |>
  bind_cols(
    lr_plot_fit |> predict(new_data),
    lr_plot_fit |> predict(new_data, 
                           type = "conf_int") |>
      rename(.conf_lower = .pred_lower,
             .conf_upper = .pred_upper),
    lr_plot_fit |> predict(new_data, 
                           type = "pred_int")
  ) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = x1, ymin = .pred_lower, 
                  ymax = .pred_upper), fill = "grey") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = x1, ymin = .conf_lower, 
                  ymax = .conf_upper), fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(aes(x = x1, y = .pred), 
            color = "blue") + 
  labs(
    title = "Model with Confidence and Prediction Intervals",
    x = "x1",
    y = "y"
  )
```

:::

:::{.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

new_data <- tibble(
  x1 = seq(0, 10, length.out = 100)
)

new_data |>
  bind_cols(
    lr_plot_fit |> predict(new_data),
    lr_plot_fit |> predict(new_data, type = "conf_int") |>
      rename(.conf_lower = .pred_lower,
             .conf_upper = .pred_upper),
    lr_plot_fit |> predict(new_data, type = "pred_int")
  ) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = x1, ymin = .pred_lower, ymax = .pred_upper), fill = "grey") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = x1, ymin = .conf_lower, ymax = .conf_upper), fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(aes(x = x1, y = .pred), color = "blue") + 
  labs(
    title = "Model with Confidence and Prediction Intervals",
    x = "x1",
    y = "y"
  )
```

```{r}

#| eval: true

  bind_cols(
    lr_plot_fit |> predict(new_data),
    lr_plot_fit |> predict(new_data, type = "conf_int") |>
      rename(.conf_lower = .pred_lower,
             .conf_upper = .pred_upper),
    lr_plot_fit |> predict(new_data, type = "pred_int")
  ) |>
  kable() |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 16) |>
```

## Summary

<div style="font-size:16pt">

:::{.fragment}

Below are the most common applications of statistical inference in regression modeling.

:::

+ Hypothesis Tests

  + **Global Test for Model Utility:** Does our model have any utility at all?
  + **Individual Term-Based Tests:** Are each of the included predictor terms useful after accounting for the other terms in the model?

+ Confidence Intervals

  + What is the plausible range for each parameter/coefficient? 
  
    + Confidence Intervals for coefficients, conditioned on other model terms.
  + Can we make reliable predictions? 
  
    + Confidence Intervals for *average response*
    + Prediction Intervals for *individual response*
    
:::{.fragment}

We'll be utilizing all of these ideas throughout our course.

:::

:::{.fragment}

We'll leverage R functionality to obtain intervals or to calculate test statistics and $p$-values though, since it is much faster and more accurate than doing any of this by hand.

:::

</div>
